name: Crab Nebula
credit: NASA, ESA, J. Hester and A. Loll
trivia: The remnant of a supernova that Chinese astronomers recorded in 1054 CE.

name: NGC 7089
trivia: Holds about 150,000 stars and is one of the larger globular clusters known.

name: NGC 5272
credit: T.A. Rector, H. Schweiker et al.
trivia: Holds more than 270 known variable stars, among the most of any globular cluster.

name: NGC 6121
trivia: One of the closest globular clusters to Earth, lying about 1.3 degrees west of Antares.

name: NGC 5904
trivia: Among the oldest globular clusters in the Milky Way, at about 13 billion years old.

name: Butterfly Cluster
trivia: Its brightest star, BM Scorpii, is an orange giant that varies in brightness.

name: Ptolemy Cluster
trivia: Ptolemy described it around 130 CE as a nebulous patch following the sting of Scorpius.

name: Lagoon Nebula
trivia: Visible to the naked eye under dark skies, it contains the bright Hourglass Nebula at its core.

name: NGC 6333
trivia: Lies only about 5,500 light-years from the Milky Way's centre, near the galactic bulge.

name: NGC 6254
trivia: M10 and M12 form a near-matching pair of globular clusters in Ophiuchus, about 3 degrees apart.

name: Wild Duck Cluster
trivia: Admiral Smyth likened its fan-shaped star pattern to a flock of ducks in flight.

name: NGC 6218
trivia: A loosely concentrated globular cluster whose core is less dense than most.

name: Great Hercules Cluster
credit: T.A. Rector, H. Schweiker et al.
trivia: The 1974 Arecibo radio message was aimed at this cluster.

name: NGC 6402
trivia: A nova appeared in this cluster in 1938, a rare event in a globular cluster.

name: NGC 7078
trivia: One of the densest known globular clusters, with a collapsed core.

name: Eagle Nebula
trivia: Contains the Pillars of Creation, famously photographed by Hubble in 1995.

name: Omega Nebula
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and WIYN
trivia: Also called the Swan or Horseshoe Nebula, it is one of the brightest star-forming regions in the Milky Way.

name: NGC 6613
trivia: A sparse cluster of about 20 stars in Sagittarius, close to the Omega Nebula in the sky.

name: NGC 6273
trivia: One of the most flattened globular clusters known, visibly oblate.

name: Trifid Nebula
trivia: Dark dust lanes divide its glowing emission nebula into three lobes.

name: NGC 6531
trivia: A young open cluster, only a few million years old, lying near the Trifid Nebula.

name: NGC 6656
trivia: One of the first globular clusters ever discovered, found by Abraham Ihle in 1665.

name: NGC 6494
trivia: Contains about 150 stars spread over an area roughly the size of the full Moon.

name: Sagittarius Star Cloud
trivia: A dense patch of the Milky Way seen through a gap in the intervening dust clouds.

name: IC 4725
credit: Hillary Mathis, Vanessa Harvey et al.
trivia: Contains the Cepheid variable U Sagittarii, a rare find in an open cluster.

name: NGC 6694
credit: Hillary Mathis, Vanessa Harvey et al.
trivia: Shows a region of unusually low star density, possibly caused by a dust cloud in front of it.

name: Dumbbell Nebula
credit: T.A. Rector, H. Schweiker et al.
trivia: The first planetary nebula ever discovered, found by Messier in 1764.

name: NGC 6626
trivia: Contains a millisecond pulsar, the first ever found in a globular cluster.

name: NGC 6913
trivia: A small cluster of about 50 stars near Gamma Cygni, nicknamed the Cooling Tower.

name: NGC 7099
trivia: Its core has collapsed, making it one of the densest globular clusters.

name: Andromeda Galaxy
trivia: Approaching the Milky Way at about 110 km/s, it is expected to merge with it in billions of years.

name: NGC 221
trivia: A compact satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, probably the stripped core of a larger galaxy.

name: Triangulum Galaxy
trivia: Contains NGC 604, one of the largest star-forming regions in the Local Group.

name: NGC 1039
trivia: Visible to the naked eye under dark skies, and roughly 250 million years old.

name: NGC 2168
trivia: The much more distant cluster NGC 2158 sits beside it and fits in the same low-power field.

name: NGC 1960
trivia: A young cluster about 25 million years old, one of three Messier clusters in Auriga.

name: NGC 2099
trivia: The richest of the three Messier open clusters in Auriga.

name: NGC 1912
trivia: Its brighter stars form a loose cross or pi shape; the small cluster NGC 1907 lies nearby.

name: NGC 7092
trivia: A roughly triangular open cluster in Cygnus, easy to see with binoculars.

name: Winnecke 4
trivia: Messier searched for a nebula reported by Hevelius and logged this double star instead.

name: NGC 2287
trivia: Lies about 4 degrees south of Sirius and was possibly noted by Aristotle around 325 BCE.

name: Orion Nebula
credit: NASA, ESA, M. Robberto et al.
trivia: The nearest massive star-forming region, visible to the naked eye in Orion's sword.

name: De Mairan's Nebula
trivia: A dark dust lane separates it from the Orion Nebula, and the star NU Orionis lights it.

name: Beehive Cluster
trivia: Galileo first resolved the Beehive Cluster, also called Praesepe, into about 40 stars with his telescope.

name: Pleiades
trivia: Its blue nebulosity is dust the cluster is passing through, not leftover birth gas.

name: NGC 2437
trivia: The planetary nebula NGC 2438 appears to lie inside it, though it is probably a foreground object.

name: NGC 2422
trivia: Long a missing Messier object because Messier recorded its position incorrectly.

name: NGC 2548
trivia: Long considered missing due to a position error, it was identified with NGC 2548 in 1934.

name: NGC 4472
trivia: The brightest elliptical galaxy in the Virgo Cluster, discovered by Messier in 1771.

name: NGC 2323
trivia: Often described as heart-shaped in photographs.

name: Whirlpool Galaxy
trivia: Lord Rosse was the first to identify its spiral structure, in 1845.

name: NGC 7654
trivia: Found in Cassiopeia by extending a line from Alpha to Beta Cassiopeiae; it lies near the Bubble Nebula.

name: NGC 5024
trivia: Lies only about 1 degree from NGC 5053, a much sparser globular cluster.

name: NGC 6715
trivia: Belongs to the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy rather than to the Milky Way itself.

name: NGC 6809
trivia: Large and loose, so many of its stars can be resolved in modest telescopes.

name: NGC 6779
trivia: Lies in a rich Milky Way star field in Lyra, between Albireo and Gamma Lyrae.

name: Ring Nebula
credit: NASA, ESA, and C. Robert O’Dell (Vanderbilt University)
trivia: A faint central white dwarf near magnitude 15 sits inside the glowing ring.

name: NGC 4579
trivia: A barred spiral and one of the brighter galaxies of the Virgo Cluster.

name: NGC 4621
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, L. Ho et al.
trivia: Discovered in 1779 by Johann Gottfried Koehler, who found M60 the same night.

name: NGC 4649
trivia: Lies next to the smaller spiral NGC 4647, with which it appears to be interacting.

name: NGC 4303
trivia: A face-on spiral that has hosted at least six observed supernovae.

name: NGC 6266
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, S. Anderson et al
trivia: One of the most asymmetrical globular clusters known, distorted by tides near the galactic centre.

name: Sunflower Galaxy
credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/Bruce Hugo and Leslie Gaul/Adam Block
trivia: Its tightly wound arms break into short segments, giving a sunflower look.

name: Black Eye Galaxy
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, J. Lee and the PHANGS-HST Team
trivia: Its outer gas rotates opposite to its inner stars, probably from an ancient merger.

name: NGC 3623
trivia: Forms the Leo Triplet with M66 and NGC 3628.

name: NGC 3627
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, J. Lee, T. Williams, PHANGS Team
trivia: Its distorted spiral arms are probably the result of gravitational interaction within the Leo Triplet.

name: NGC 2682
trivia: One of the oldest known open clusters, about 4 billion years old, close to the Sun's age.

name: NGC 4590
trivia: A very metal-poor globular cluster in Hydra.

name: NGC 6637
trivia: Discovered by Nicolas Lacaille in 1751-52 and added to Messier's catalogue in 1780.

name: NGC 6681
trivia: Messier observed it on the same night as M69 in August 1780.

name: NGC 6838
trivia: Long debated as a loose globular or dense open cluster, it is now classed as a globular.

name: NGC 6981
trivia: Found by Pierre Mechain in 1780, along with the nearby M73.

name: NGC 6994
trivia: Not a true cluster but a chance alignment of four stars in Aquarius.

name: Phantom Galaxy
trivia: A textbook face-on spiral, but its low surface brightness makes it hard to see.

name: NGC 6864
trivia: One of the most highly concentrated globular clusters, with a very dense core.

name: Little Dumbbell Nebula
trivia: Called the Little Dumbbell for its resemblance to M27, it is among the faintest Messier objects.

name: NGC 1068
trivia: A Seyfert galaxy whose neutrino emission was reported by IceCube in 2022.

name: NGC 2068
trivia: The brightest diffuse reflection nebula in the sky, in Orion.

name: NGC 1904
trivia: May have been captured from the Canis Major Dwarf Galaxy.

name: NGC 6093
trivia: One of the densest globular clusters; a nova, T Scorpii, appeared in it in 1860.

name: Bode's Galaxy
trivia: Discovered by Johann Elert Bode in 1774, it forms a pair in the sky with M82.

name: Cigar Galaxy
credit: NASA, ESA, and The Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)
trivia: A starburst galaxy forming stars about ten times faster than the Milky Way.

name: Southern Pinwheel Galaxy
trivia: It has hosted at least six observed supernovae.

name: NGC 4374
trivia: Hosts a supermassive black hole of more than a billion solar masses.

name: NGC 4382
trivia: A lenticular galaxy whose faint shells suggest a past merger; Mechain found it in 1781.

name: NGC 4406
trivia: One of the few Virgo Cluster galaxies moving toward us, as it falls toward the cluster's centre.

name: Virgo A
trivia: Its black hole was the first ever imaged, by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019.

name: NGC 4501
trivia: A large spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices, discovered by Messier in 1781.

name: NGC 4552
trivia: A nearly spherical elliptical galaxy surrounded by faint shells.

name: NGC 4569
trivia: One of the few galaxies in the Virgo Cluster that is blueshifted, moving toward us.

name: NGC 4548
trivia: Long missing from the catalogue, it was identified with NGC 4548 in 1969.

name: NGC 6341
trivia: One of the brighter northern globular clusters, often overlooked beside M13 in Hercules.

name: NGC 2447
trivia: A bright open cluster in Puppis with a wedge or arrowhead shape.

name: NGC 4736
credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/SAO; Optical: Brian Brennan and Remi Lacasse
trivia: A starburst galaxy with a bright inner ring of intense star formation.

name: NGC 3351
trivia: A barred spiral with a ring of star formation, in the Leo I Group with M96.

name: NGC 3368
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA and the LEGUS Team
trivia: Lends its name to the M96 Group of galaxies in Leo, which includes M95 and M105.

name: Owl Nebula
trivia: Lord Rosse named it in 1848 for two dark patches that resemble an owl's eyes.

name: NGC 4192
trivia: Seen nearly edge-on, it is blueshifted, approaching us as it falls into the Virgo Cluster.

name: NGC 4254
trivia: Lord Rosse identified its spiral structure in 1846, a year after M51.

name: NGC 4321
trivia: A grand-design spiral whose Cepheid variables helped Hubble calibrate the distance scale.

name: Pinwheel Galaxy
credit: George Jacoby, Bruce Bohannan, Mark Hanna/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA
trivia: About 170,000 light-years across, it is larger than the Milky Way.

name: Spindle Galaxy
credit: NASA, ESA, and The Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)
trivia: Its identity as M102 is disputed, and Messier's entry may be a duplicate of M101.

name: NGC 581
trivia: Discovered by Pierre Mechain in 1781; the cluster is only about 25 million years old.

name: Sombrero Galaxy
trivia: Its prominent dust lane and large central bulge give it the look of a wide-brimmed hat.

name: NGC 3379
trivia: An elliptical galaxy in the Leo I Group, near M95 and M96.

name: NGC 4258
trivia: Water-maser emission in its disc gave a precise geometric distance used to calibrate the cosmic scale.

name: NGC 6171
trivia: Pierre Mechain discovered it in April 1782 in Ophiuchus.

name: Surfboard Galaxy
trivia: Seen nearly edge-on, it hosted the supernova SN 1969B.

name: NGC 3992
trivia: A barred spiral that hosted the supernova SN 1956A.

name: NGC 205
trivia: Kenneth Glyn Jones added it to the Messier list in 1967.

name: NGC 188
trivia: One of the oldest known open clusters, about 7 billion years old, near the north celestial pole.

name: Bow-Tie Nebula
trivia: The central star is a Wolf-Rayet-type star shedding material that forms the glowing shell.

name: NGC 4236
trivia: A barred spiral in Draco with low surface brightness, so it needs a dark sky.

name: Iris Nebula
trivia: A reflection nebula lit by the young star HD 200775.

name: Hidden Galaxy
credit: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/T.A. Rector & H. Schweiker et al.
trivia: Milky Way dust hides much of its light; it would otherwise rank among the brightest galaxies.

name: Cat's Eye Nebula
trivia: In 1864 William Huggins showed from its spectrum that planetary nebulae are glowing gas.

name: NGC 2403
trivia: Contains NGC 2404, one of the largest known star-forming regions.

name: NGC 559
trivia: Discovered by William Herschel in 1787.

name: Cave Nebula
credit: T.A. Rector, H. Schweiker et al.
trivia: A faint emission nebula in Cepheus whose dark lane gives the cave-mouth look.

name: NGC 663
trivia: Contains a number of Be stars, hot and rapidly spinning.

name: Bubble Nebula
trivia: The bubble is blown by the stellar wind of the star BD+60 2522.

name: Fireworks Galaxy
trivia: Ten supernovae have been observed in it since 1917, earning the nickname.

name: Owl Cluster
trivia: Two bright stars look like eyes, giving the nicknames Owl Cluster and E.T. Cluster.

name: Double Cluster
trivia: Both clusters are visible to the naked eye and are each about 13 million years old.

name: Blinking Planetary
trivia: Look straight at it and the bright central star drowns the nebula, which reappears when you glance away.

name: NGC 7243
trivia: A bright, loose open cluster in Lacerta, easily seen in binoculars.

name: NGC 147
trivia: A dwarf satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, paired with NGC 185.

name: NGC 185
trivia: A dwarf elliptical satellite of Andromeda that unusually contains dust and young stars.

name: Cocoon Nebula
trivia: The dark nebula Barnard 168 stretches westward from it like a long tail.

name: North America Nebula
trivia: Its shape resembles North America, and it lies next to the bright star Deneb.

name: NGC 4449
trivia: Hubble images show many young star clusters in this irregular starburst galaxy.

name: Blue Snowball Nebula
trivia: Its blue-green colour and round shape give it the nickname Blue Snowball.

name: NGC 891
trivia: A near-perfect edge-on spiral with a thin dust lane, often compared to the Milky Way.

name: Perseus A
trivia: The central galaxy of the Perseus Cluster, wrapped in filaments of gas and a strong radio source.

name: Intergalactic Wanderer
trivia: One of the most remote globular clusters of the Milky Way; Shapley called it the Intergalactic Tramp.

name: Silver Needle Galaxy
trivia: Seen edge-on and slightly warped, it is a pure disc galaxy with no noticeable bulge.

name: Crescent Nebula
trivia: Blown by the Wolf-Rayet star WR 136, which will eventually end as a supernova.

name: NGC 752
trivia: An old open cluster over a billion years old, large enough to fill a binocular field.

name: NGC 5005
trivia: A spiral in Canes Venatici with a LINER-type active nucleus.

name: NGC 7331
trivia: Often called a Milky Way twin; Stephan's Quintet appears nearby in the sky but is far more distant.

name: Flaming Star Nebula
trivia: Lit by the runaway star AE Aurigae.

name: Whale Galaxy
trivia: Seen edge-on, its disc is distorted and starburst-active, probably from interaction with neighbours.

name: Eastern Veil Nebula
trivia: Part of the Cygnus Loop, the remnant of a supernova that exploded 10,000 to 20,000 years ago.

name: Western Veil Nebula
trivia: Its brightest part is crossed by the foreground star 52 Cygni.

name: NGC 4889
trivia: The brightest galaxy in the Coma Cluster, with a black hole estimated at about 21 billion solar masses.

name: NGC 4559
trivia: Discovered by William Herschel in 1785.

name: NGC 6885
trivia: An open cluster in Vulpecula containing the star 20 Vulpeculae.

name: Needle Galaxy
trivia: A near-perfect edge-on spiral with a thin dust lane, a favourite of amateurs in Coma Berenices.

name: Eskimo Nebula
trivia: From the ground it looks like a face in a fur parka, and Hubble reveals a complex gas outflow.

name: NGC 3626
trivia: A lenticular galaxy in Leo whose gas and stars rotate in opposite directions.

name: Hyades
trivia: The nearest open cluster to the Sun, forming the V-shaped face of Taurus the Bull.

name: NGC 7006
trivia: One of the most distant globular clusters of the Milky Way, lying in the outer halo.

name: Little Sombrero
trivia: Its central bulge and dust lane resemble the Sombrero Galaxy on a smaller scale.

name: Propeller Galaxy
trivia: Its single prominent arm is thought to come from a past minor merger with a smaller galaxy.

name: NGC 5248
trivia: A grand-design spiral in Bootes with a ring of star formation around its core.

name: Hubble's Variable Nebula
trivia: Its brightness and shape change within weeks as clouds shade light from the variable star R Monocerotis.

name: NGC 6934
trivia: Discovered by William Herschel in 1785.

name: NGC 2775
trivia: Dust lanes spiral around a smooth, bright central bulge.

name: Rosette Nebula
trivia: Stellar winds from the young cluster NGC 2244 have cleared the hole at its centre.

name: Rosette Cluster
trivia: A young open cluster whose hot stars ionise the surrounding Rosette Nebula.

name: IC 1613
trivia: A Local Group dwarf galaxy with few dust clouds, a good laboratory for Cepheid variable stars.

name: NGC 4697
trivia: Discovered by William Herschel in 1784.

name: Spindle Galaxy
trivia: A lenticular galaxy hosting one of the nearest known billion-solar-mass black holes.

name: NGC 2506
trivia: An old open cluster, over a billion years old, in Monoceros.

name: Saturn Nebula
trivia: Lord Rosse's drawing showed bright extensions like Saturn's rings, hence the name.

name: Skull Nebula
trivia: Its nickname comes from dark patches and stars that suggest eyes and a nose.

name: Barnard's Galaxy
trivia: Hubble used it in 1925 to help show that galaxies exist beyond the Milky Way.

name: Caroline's Cluster
trivia: Discovered by Caroline Herschel in 1783.

name: Ghost of Jupiter
trivia: Its nickname comes from its apparent size, similar to Jupiter's disc in a small telescope.

name: Antennae Galaxies
trivia: NGC 4038, the northern Antennae galaxy, holds most of the pair's bright pink knots of new stars.

name: Antennae Galaxies
trivia: NGC 4039, the southern Antennae galaxy, is merging with NGC 4038 and the two will become one galaxy.

name: NGC 247
trivia: A member of the Sculptor Group that shows a notable clear gap in its disc.

name: Helix Nebula
trivia: One of the closest planetary nebulae to Earth.

name: Tau Canis Majoris Cluster
trivia: A very young open cluster, only a few million years old, around Tau Canis Majoris.

name: Sculptor Galaxy
trivia: One of the brightest spiral galaxies in the sky, discovered by Caroline Herschel in 1783.

name: NGC 5694
trivia: Discovered by William Herschel in 1784, it lies in the Milky Way's outer halo.

name: NGC 1097
trivia: A barred spiral with a bright starburst ring around its core and a small satellite galaxy.

name: NGC 6729
trivia: A comet-shaped nebula in Corona Australis surrounding the variable star R Coronae Australis.

name: Bug Nebula
credit: NASA, ESA, and the Hubble SM4 ERO Team
trivia: Its central star is among the hottest known, at over 200,000 K.

name: NGC 300
trivia: A member of the Sculptor Group seen almost face-on, one of the nearest spirals beyond the Local Group.

name: NGC 2477
trivia: One of the richest open clusters in Puppis, with several hundred stars.

name: NGC 55
trivia: Seen nearly edge-on, it is an irregular barred spiral in the Sculptor Group.

name: NGC 1851
trivia: A dense globular cluster in Columba with evidence of two distinct stellar populations.

name: Southern Ring Nebula
trivia: Webb's 2022 images show the fainter of its two central stars shaped the nebula.

name: NGC 6124
trivia: A bright open cluster in Scorpius found by Lacaille in 1751-52.

name: NGC 6231
trivia: The heart of the Scorpius OB1 association, packed with luminous O and B stars.

name: Centaurus A
trivia: A galaxy merger with a prominent dust lane and a powerful radio jet, and one of the nearest active galaxies.

name: NGC 6541
trivia: A core-collapsed globular cluster in Corona Australis.

name: NGC 3201
trivia: A stellar-mass black hole was found in it in 2018 by tracking a companion star's motion.

name: Omega Centauri
trivia: The most massive globular cluster in the Milky Way, probably the stripped core of a dwarf galaxy.

name: NGC 6352
trivia: A metal-rich globular cluster in Ara discovered by James Dunlop in 1826.

name: NGC 6193
trivia: Its hot stars light up the neighbouring emission nebula NGC 6188.

name: NGC 4945
trivia: A Milky Way-like barred spiral seen edge-on, with a hidden active nucleus.

name: NGC 5286
trivia: A globular cluster in Centaurus discovered by James Dunlop in 1826.

name: Omicron Velorum Cluster
trivia: A bright, nearby open cluster visible to the naked eye.

name: NGC 6397
trivia: Among the closest globular clusters to Earth.

name: NGC 1261
trivia: A southern globular cluster in Horologium, discovered by James Dunlop in 1826.

name: NGC 5823
credit: Legacy Surveys / D. Lang (Perimeter Institute), Meli thev
trivia: A rich open cluster in the southern constellation Circinus, in a dense Milky Way field.

name: S Normae Cluster
trivia: Contains the Cepheid variable S Normae, a bright supergiant member.

name: NGC 2867
trivia: A compact planetary nebula in Carina with a hot central star.

name: Wishing Well Cluster
trivia: One of the brightest and richest open clusters, with some 400 stars, visible to the naked eye.

name: Carina Nebula
trivia: Contains Eta Carinae, which erupted in the 1840s to become the second-brightest star in the sky.

name: NGC 6752
trivia: The third-brightest globular cluster in the sky, nicknamed the Great Peacock Globular.

name: Jewel Box
trivia: John Herschel likened its coloured stars to a casket of jewels.

name: NGC 6025
trivia: An open cluster in Triangulum Australe, discovered by Lacaille in 1751-52.

name: Southern Beehive Cluster
trivia: Bright enough to see with the naked eye in Carina.

name: Pearl Cluster
trivia: A young open cluster in Centaurus, about 20 million years old, with many B-type stars.

name: NGC 4609
trivia: A small open cluster in Crux, next to the Coalsack.

name: Coalsack Nebula
trivia: The most prominent dark nebula in the sky, visible to the naked eye beside the Southern Cross.

name: Lambda Centauri Nebula
trivia: Its dark globules were identified in 1950 by A. D. Thackeray.

name: NGC 6744
credit: Dark Energy Survey / NOIRLab / NSF / AURA
trivia: Often called a Milky Way twin for its size and structure, in Pavo.

name: Southern Pleiades
trivia: Its brightest star, Theta Carinae, makes the cluster visible to the naked eye.

name: Tarantula Nebula
trivia: The most active starburst region in the Local Group, in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

name: NGC 362
trivia: Appears beside the Small Magellanic Cloud in Tucana but is far closer to us.

name: NGC 4833
trivia: A dusty, heavily reddened globular cluster in Musca, found by Lacaille in 1751-52.

name: 47 Tucanae
trivia: The second-brightest globular cluster in the sky after Omega Centauri.

name: NGC 6101
trivia: A remote, loose globular cluster in Apus, discovered by James Dunlop in 1826.

name: NGC 4372
trivia: A loose globular cluster in Musca, near the dark nebula known as the Dark Doodad.

name: NGC 3195
trivia: A planetary nebula in Chamaeleon, and the last entry in the Caldwell list.
